name: Artemisinin
short: Case reports: hepatitis and severe cholestatic liver injury with artemisinin supplements. Related antimalarial drugs show considerable toxicity in animals, including harm to embryos.
text: Case reports describe liver injury with herbal supplements containing artemisinin: a 2008 US public health report described a patient who developed hepatitis (ALT 898 IU/L) after a 1-week course; testing found the stated artemisinin content and no other common pharmaceutical ingredients, and investigators concluded that the hepatitis might have been associated with the supplement but that more data are needed to establish a causal connection. Other case reports describe severe cholestatic liver injury from an artemisinin-containing supplement, treated with plasma exchange, with bilirubin returning to baseline after 62 days, and a probable immune-mediated liver injury in a woman having radiotherapy for a pelvic sarcoma, which improved with oral corticosteroids; a further report is titled as describing cholestatic liver injury secondary to artemisinin (no abstract). A related product, Artemisia annua tea taken to prevent malaria, was linked to severe acute cholestatic hepatitis, rated a probable cause, in a traveller returning from Ethiopia; analysis of the tea found arteannuin B, deoxyartemisin, camphor and scopoletin, and the abstract does not list artemisinin among its ingredients. Most other safety data concern artemisinin-derived antimalarial medicines (such as artesunate and artemether), not supplements: a toxicology review reports that large clinical studies and meta-analyses did not show serious side effects but that there are too few large trials to detect rare but significant toxicity, while animal experiments show considerable toxicity, with the review covering neurotoxicity, embryotoxicity, genotoxicity, toxicity to blood, immune system, heart and kidney, and allergic reactions; it adds that rapid elimination after taking artemisinins by mouth is a relatively safe route compared with delayed drug release after intramuscular injection. The World Health Organization does not recommend these derivatives in the first trimester of pregnancy because of embryolethality and teratogenic effects in non-clinical studies, which a review says have not been proved in humans; a meta-analysis of 20 studies, with 3,707 women treated, found no increased risk of congenital malformations or miscarriage with treatment in the second or third trimester. For interactions, two reviews of artemisinin-based combination antimalarials report pharmacokinetic interactions with HIV medicines (one names protease inhibitors and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors), and one of them states that, based on known genotypes of the enzymes, CYP2B6 and CYP3A are primarily involved in the metabolism of artemisinin and its derivatives; the abstracts do not report interaction studies with artemisinin supplements.
